Its ring equals the predecessor coastal outer ring after the Kandyan hole is removed. The British East India Company bbox overlaps, but polygon intersection testing is false.

sources.note: Decoded with topojson-client. The successor sri-lanka feature is a 35-position Polygon with the same broad island outline. The maximum paired coordinate difference from the last colonial ring is about 0.0012003 degrees, so this is a near-continuous atlas handoff, not an exact coordinate identity or a correct independence date.

sources.title: UK National Archives, Colonial administration records: Ceylon
sources.note: Official guide checked. It states that the British colony was established in 1802, the entire island came under British control after the annexation of Kandy in 1815, and Ceylon became a self-governing Commonwealth state in 1948. It also identifies relevant Colonial and Dominions Office record series.

sources.title: Sri Lanka National Archives, 1815 Convention
sources.note: National Archives exhibit and cited signature page checked. British control of former Dutch coastal territories preceded the March 1815 Convention; Article 4 transferred Kandyan sovereignty and Article 5 promised protection of the Buddhist order and customs. The exhibit describes political manoeuvring among British officials and Kandyan chiefs.

sources.title: Sri Lanka National Archives, Sir John D'Oyly, the Strategist
sources.note: Exhibit and archival locator checked. D'Oyly drafted the Convention, studied Sinhala language and literature, cultivated clerical and literary contacts, and was employed as a British spy to create discord between the Kandyan king and nobility.

sources.title: Sri Lanka National Archives, Freedom Struggle, 1818
sources.note: Exhibit checked against cited governor letters and Gazette. Resistance spread through Kandyan regions from 1817; the British captured leaders and the Tooth Relic, suppressed the revolt ruthlessly, and branded nineteen chiefs traitors in a proclamation later invalidated in 2016.

sources.title: Sri Lanka National Archives, The First Reforms, 1833
sources.note: Exhibit and Colebrooke-Cameron records checked. Recommendations included Executive and Legislative Councils, five provinces, a new islandwide judicial system, unofficial representation of Sinhalese, Tamils and Burghers, and abolition of rajakariya compulsory labour.

sources.title: Sri Lanka National Archives, Freedom Struggle, 1848
sources.note: Exhibit checked against cited petition, despatches, Gazette and 1840 ordinance. Dumbara petitioners said the Road Ordinance restored compulsory labour; about 3,000 unarmed people gathered at Kandy, objecting to taxes. The exhibit links possible ancestral-land loss to the Crown Lands Encroachment Ordinance and records martial law as protest became violent.

sources.title: Sri Lanka National Archives, Introducing the Elective Principle
sources.note: Exhibit checked. The 1910 Crewe-McCallum reforms introduced a very limited elective element: the Legislative Council had eleven officials and ten non-officials, only four elected on an ethnic basis. Ponnambalam Ramanathan became the first educated representative selected through the new arrangement.

sources.title: Sri Lanka National Archives, Hundred Days of Terror
sources.note: Exhibit checked against cited police material. During the 1915 riots, martial law from 2 June allowed police and army to shoot alleged rioters without trial or showing cause; Edward Henry Pedris was court-martialled and executed, and Sinhala leaders were imprisoned. The page foregrounds colonial repression and is not a complete history of intercommunal harms.

sources.title: Sri Lanka National Archives, Ceylon National Congress
sources.note: Exhibit checked. The Congress was founded on 11 December 1919 with Ponnambalam Arunachalam as first president and sought a common constitutional movement. Disputes over representation and later departures weakened it and damaged trust between Sinhala and Tamil leaders.

sources.title: Sri Lanka National Archives, Labour Movement
sources.note: Exhibit checked. It records resistance to a road contribution requiring adult men to work six days, founding of the Ceylon Labour Union in 1922, the 1923 general strike, and A.E. Gunasinghe advocacy of adult suffrage regardless of gender, race, religion or caste.

sources.title: Sri Lanka National Archives, Donoughmore Commission, 1931
sources.note: Exhibit checked against cited 1927 testimony and 1931 Hansard. Donoughmore changes brought universal suffrage, territorial representation, a State Council, executive committees and ministers. Evidence from Agnes de Silva and other Society for Women's Suffrage members helped secure women's voting rights.

sources.title: Sri Lanka National Archives, Bracegirdle Case
sources.note: Exhibit checked against the 1937 commission locator. Plantation manager Mark Bracegirdle opposed long hours and reported brutal treatment of workers, including women and children; his ordered deportation became a labour-political confrontation reviewed by the State Council.

sources.title: Sri Lanka National Archives, Suriya-Mal Movement
sources.note: Exhibit checked. Founded in 1933 with Doreen Wickramasinghe as president, the anti-imperial welfare movement worked on education for children treated as lower caste and delivered medicine, food and other aid during the malaria crisis. The page is a National Archives interpretation of movement records.

sources.title: Sri Lanka National Archives, Dominion Status
sources.note: Exhibit checked against the Ceylon Independence Act and related records. The British Parliament passed the Act in November 1947; Ceylon was declared an independent state on 4 February 1948. That date, rather than the atlas endpoint of 1945, ends British colonial rule.

sources.title: Parliament of Sri Lanka, Evolution of the Parliamentary System
sources.note: Official parliamentary history checked. It distinguishes the 1833-1931 Legislative Council, 1931-1947 State Council and later House of Representatives, and dates the Soulbury Commission Westminster model to 1944. These institutions expanded representation within, and then beyond, colonial rule.

sources.title: Sri Lanka Tea Board, History of Ceylon Tea
sources.note: Official industry history checked. It describes state-supported coffee expansion, road building and forest conversion in the central hills, the 1869 appearance of coffee rust, and the collapse of coffee within about a decade. Its celebratory language about colonial prosperity requires comparison with labour and rural-economy evidence.

sources.title: Sri Lanka Tea Board, Tea Saves the Day
sources.note: Industry history checked. James Taylor experimented with tea processing by 1866, planted twenty acres at Loolecondera and shipped a first 23-pound consignment. The page calls him the first successful Ceylon planter, not the first person to attempt tea; it is a planter-centred account.

sources.title: Wenzlhuemer, Indian Labour Immigration and British Labour Policy in Nineteenth-Century Ceylon
sources.note: Peer-reviewed Modern Asian Studies abstract checked. Coffee and tea export monocultures depended overwhelmingly on imported South Indian wage labour. The kangany system organized migration and labour supply while government regulation remained slight for much of the nineteenth century.

sources.title: Sri Lanka Railways, History
sources.note: Official railway history checked. Rail began in 1864 to move hill-country coffee to Colombo, expanded for tea and other plantations, and carried labour, machinery, manure, rice and food. It later served broader passenger travel; the original export purpose remains important context.

sources.title: Central Bank of Sri Lanka, 25th Anniversary Review of the Economy
sources.note: Official retrospective checked. It distinguishes an export plantation sector from rural subsistence food production, says rural gains from plantation growth were negligible, identifies immigrant South Indian labour, and reports that more than 90 percent of colonial-era exports were plantation products while imports were largely consumer goods including food.

sources.title: FAO, Modernization in irrigation-system rehabilitation in Sri Lanka
sources.note: FAO technical paper checked. Sri Lankan irrigation systems have histories exceeding two millennia; British colonial governments renovated many systems to promote irrigated agriculture. Renovation is therefore distinguished from invention of the island's ancient hydraulic heritage.

sources.title: FAO, Research area: agricultural background in Sri Lanka
sources.note: FAO study checked. It describes a dry-zone pattern in which irrigable land often grew rice mainly for home consumption while dry land produced subsidiary foods for both market and household. This later study is used cautiously as a pattern, not a census of colonial meals.

sources.title: World Bank, Tackling Chronic Undernutrition in Sri Lanka's Plantations
sources.note: World Bank feature checked. A plantation-workers museum occupies line rooms more than a century old and reconstructs an approximately 100-square-foot home with clay walls, pots, pans and a basic hearth. It is a modern museum reconstruction, not a complete survey of every estate household.

sources.title: Sri Lanka LawNet, Perera v. Aselin Nona, New Law Reports vol. 60
sources.note: Later appellate judgment checked for its explanation of older Kandyan law. In a binna marriage the husband lived in the wife's parental home and she retained inheritance rights; in diga she moved to the husband's home and usually lost parental inheritance, subject to exceptions. This is Kandyan legal history, not an islandwide family rule.

sources.title: British Museum, Sri Lankan shore-seine fishing-boat model As1933,1110.4
sources.note: Museum catalog checked. The nineteenth- to twentieth-century ma-del-paru model documents a flat-bottomed shore-seine boat: wood planks were sewn in a criss-cross pattern with coconut-fibre rope and seams caulked with leaves. Curators locate variants on west, south and northeast coasts; provenance beyond an old Ceylon label is limited.

sources.title: British Museum, Sri Lankan dance mask As,+.2764
sources.note: Museum catalog checked. The painted wood mask is dated to the nineteenth century and assigned to Sri Lanka's interior; its colonial register describes cobra forms. It was purchased from a dealer in 1886, so it evidences an object and collecting history, not every dance or community.

sources.title: British Museum, robe collection catalogue
sources.note: Museum catalogue index checked. It lists several Buddhist garment, robe and cloth objects acquired in Sri Lanka, including As1908,0521.2-.4. The index supplies religious and acquisition associations but little production context; it cannot support a single national costume.

sources.title: British Museum, Collecting and Empire trail
sources.note: Museum trail checked. It explains that colonial civil servant Hugh Nevill amassed objects with sparse provenance and likely acquired a nineteenth-century betel-nut cutter through the Kandyan Society of Arts. The object records local craft and colonial collecting together.

sources.title: UNESCO-hosted Sri Lanka education historical overview
sources.note: Historical overview checked. It describes temple-associated oral and memorized learning, later ola-leaf manuscripts and libraries, and pirivena monastic colleges serving clergy and some male lay students. These traditions predated and continued through colonial change; access was not universal.

sources.title: UNESCO IIEP, Sri Lanka Education for All National Action Plan
sources.note: Government education plan hosted by UNESCO checked. It describes British mass education as a dual system of church-assisted English schools favoured by elites and state vernacular schools for common people, alongside pirivenas; the Department of Public Instruction was established in 1869.

sources.title: Sri Lanka National Archives, Our Catalogues
sources.note: Official holdings guide checked. Relevant records include the Board of Kandyan Commissioners 1815-1833, Colebrooke-Cameron inquiry records, Jaffna and Kandy Kachcheri records, Ceylon National Congress collections, newspapers, maps, the 1818 rebellion and archaeology papers. Survival in an archive is selective evidence, not a full record of ordinary lives.

sources.title: Department of Archaeology Sri Lanka, History
sources.note: Official institutional history checked. Government surveys and photographs began in the 1860s-1870s, inscription work followed, and the department began duties in 1890 under H.C.P. Bell. It records 1897 mural finds at Sigiriya and Polonnaruwa and labels the early phase colonial.

sources.title: Department of Archaeology Sri Lanka proceedings, Decolonizing the Narration of Sri Lankan Archaeology
sources.note: Department-hosted conference paper checked. It argues that the 1890 archaeology department followed Western frameworks and excluded local voices, and calls for interpretation alongside local texts and knowledge. This provides an explicit limit on triumphalist accounts of colonial archaeology.

sources.title: Sri Lanka Ministry of Health, History of Medicine in Sri Lanka
sources.note: Official historical overview checked. Early British medical institutions were under military control; a separate Civil Medical Department was created in 1858 to provide civilian facilities. The page also notes older local medical histories and earlier Portuguese and Dutch military hospitals.

sources.title: Department of Ayurveda, National Traditional Medicine Policy
sources.note: Official 2024 policy checked for the named plurality of living systems: Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and Deshiya Chikitsa. Its ancient-history claims include policy rhetoric and are not used here; the document supports continuity and diversity rather than a single timeless practice.

sources.title: Sri Lanka Ministry of Health, Annual Health Bulletin 2024
sources.note: Official bulletin published in 2026 checked for its historical timeline. It dates Colombo Medical College to 1870, a local nursing school to 1878, women's admission to the medical college to 1892, the bacteriology laboratory to 1900, civil birth/death registration to 1867 and the census to 1871.

sources.title: Colombo Municipal Council, Greater Colombo Wastewater Management
sources.note: Official municipal page checked. Colombo sewerage planning began in 1896, construction in 1906 and major completion by 1925. The page also shows that even a 1972 regional plan found limited public-sewer coverage, so the colonial works must not be generalized to every household or town.

sources.title: Colombo Public Health Department, Administration Report 1917
sources.note: Public-domain municipal report scan checked at page 13. It urged connecting latrines to sewers and reducing flies, manure and refuse near homes to combat enteric fever, dysentery and infant diarrhoea. This is colonial public-health evidence for Colombo and contains official assumptions, not residents' voices.

sources.title: Ceylon Director of Medical and Sanitary Services, Report 1928
sources.note: Public-domain official report scan checked. Inspectors visited 3,106 schools serving 554,595 children; the report counted 2,649 schools with latrines, 493 with urinals and 991 with protected wells and still judged sanitation inadequate. Counts reflect the colonial department's categories and coverage.

sources.title: WHO, Driven to End Malaria: Ten years of success for Sri Lanka
sources.note: WHO historical review dated 24 April 2026 checked. The 1934-1935 epidemic affected about 1.5 million people and caused nearly 80,000 deaths. Responses included quinine, mobile units, environmental management, larviciding, oiling and Paris green; modern insecticide DDT came later.

sources.title: Noolaham Foundation, Uthaya Tharakai / Morning Star, 15 April 1841
sources.note: Digital heritage record checked. It identifies a twelve-page Tamil-English issue published 15 April 1841 and displays the Tamil title உதய தாரகை with English Morning Star. The newspaper came from a Jaffna mission-print context; its title is not a sample of everyone's speech.

sources.title: British Library Archives, American Ceylon Mission tracts EAP835/3/1
sources.note: Archive catalogue checked. It describes ninety-five Jaffna mission-press tracts from 1841-1891, mostly in Tamil, and transliterates the title as utayatārakai. It distinguishes translations from original compositions and documents the missionary production context.

sources.title: Unicode Standard 18.0, Tamil script
sources.note: Current Unicode 18.0 core specification checked on 27 September 2026. Tamil descends from the South Indian branch of Brahmi, is used in Sri Lanka, and is encoded with an abugida model in which consonants carry an inherent vowel that the pulli can cancel. This is script structure, not a claim that all Tamil readers pronounce words identically.

sources.title: British Museum, brass box with Tamil inscription As1895,-.130
sources.note: Museum catalog checked. A hinged brass box acquired in Kandy and purchased in 1895 carries a Tamil inscription. The catalogue supplies no production date, transcription or translation, so it proves a labelled inscribed object but cannot furnish the card's translated language sample.

proposedOverrides.summary: British colonial Ceylon after the 1815 takeover of Kandy: conquest, resistance, plantations, labour, daily life, health, education, writing and the atlas's early 1945 handoff.

batchIdentityNotes: Targeted only id ceylon-1815. The record is name Ceylon, circa 1815-1945, kind state, datesApproximate true, and missing a card before integration.

The exact target intervals are 1815-1878, 1878-1880, 1880-1900, 1900-1914, 1914-1920, 1920-1930, 1930-1938 and 1938-1945. Every feature is one 35-position Polygon; three exact coordinate variants occur across the eight snapshots.

The world-1800 predecessor ceylon-dutch-1800 is a two-ring island Polygon. Its outer ring exactly equals the world-1815 target outer ring and its interior hole exactly equals the separate Kandy Polygon. The topology expresses the atlas merger of a coastal feature and Kandyan interior.

The predecessor label Ceylon (Dutch) is historically misleading for 1800-1815: Britain acquired the former Dutch coastal territories in 1796 and established a Crown colony in 1802. This bundle does not propagate the atlas label as a historical government name.

At 1815 the British East India Company mainland bbox overlaps the island bbox; later the British Raj and one India-shaped united-kingdom-1938 occurrence do the same. Exact segment and containment tests find no polygon intersection in any target snapshot. Mysore and Travancore are nearby but disjoint.

The world-1945 sri-lanka successor is a near-identical 35-position island outline, with maximum paired coordinate delta about 0.0012003 degrees from the last target ring. This is an atlas handoff, not evidence that independence occurred in 1945.

Historical identity is British colonial Ceylon after the 1815 annexation/takeover of Kandy, within a colony established in 1802. Independence occurred on 4 February 1948. Earlier island peoples and polities and later Sri Lanka remain separate records and histories.
No appliesTo field is included because this is a single indexed record and no other record is being made to share its card.
